force: a push or a pull
gravity: the force that pulls things towards the Earth
friction: the force that slows things when surfaces rub
lever: a bar that turns on a fixed point to lift a heavy load
ramp: a slope that makes lifting easier
pulley: a wheel with a rope, used to lift loads
gear: a toothed wheel that turns another wheel

Every single time something in the world starts to move, stops moving, or changes direction, a force has acted on it. And a force is a wonderfully simple idea: it is just a push or a pull. That is all. Kick a ball, push a door, pull a rope, and you are putting a force to work.

image.note: A child kicking a ball (push) and pulling a wagon (pull), forces drawn as arrows

pages.text: Nothing moves itself. A still ball stays still until something pushes it. A moving ball keeps going until something, the ground, the air, a foot, pushes back. If you ever see a change of movement, look for the force behind it. It is always there, even when you cannot see what is doing the pushing.

image.note: A ball at rest, then kicked, then stopped by a wall; arrows showing the force at each stage

chapters.title: The Force That Holds Us Down

pages.text: One force pulls on you every second of your life, so steadily that you forget it. It is gravity, the pull of the Earth. Gravity is why a dropped mango falls, why you come back down when you jump, and why you are not floating off into the sky right now. The whole planet is quietly pulling you to itself.

image.note: A mango falling from a tree; a jumping child coming back down; downward arrows of gravity

pages.text: Gravity pulls harder on heavier things, which is why a rock is hard to lift and a leaf is not. Out in space, far from the Earth, astronauts feel almost no gravity and float freely inside their craft. It is only here, near a great heavy planet, that everything has a firm and constant down. Gravity gives your world its floor.

image.note: Split image: a child struggling to lift a rock on Earth; an astronaut drifting in a craft in space

pages.text: There is another force at work all the time, one that pushes against movement. It is called friction, and it appears wherever two surfaces rub together. Friction is why a rolling ball slows and stops, why you can walk without slipping, and why rubbing your hands together makes them warm.

image.note: A ball rolling to a stop on rough ground; hands rubbed together with heat lines; friction shown

pages.text: Friction can be friend or foe. Without it, you could not grip anything or even stand up; a world with no friction would be like standing on wet ice everywhere. But friction also wears things out and wastes energy as heat, which is why machines are oiled, to let their parts slip past each other more smoothly.

image.note: A child slipping on smooth wet tiles (too little friction) beside gripping shoes on rough ground

pages.text: Now for the clever part. People are not very strong. We cannot lift a great rock or move a heavy load with bare arms. So long ago, humans invented tools that let a small force do a big job. We call them simple machines, and they do not make energy. They just spread it out so it is easier to use.

image.note: A person unable to lift a huge rock by hand, thinking hard; a lightbulb of an idea

pages.text: A simple machine will not do work for free. If it lets you push with less force, you must push for a longer distance to make up for it. You never get something for nothing. But by trading a big effort over a short way for a small effort over a long way, a weak person can move a mighty load. That trade is the whole trick.

image.note: A balance drawn as a see-saw: small force over long distance equals big force over short distance

pages.text: The oldest simple machine is the lever. Rest a long pole across a fixed point and push down on the far end, and you can lift something far too heavy to lift by hand. A see-saw is a lever. So is a spoon prising off a tight lid. Give me a lever long enough, an old thinker once said, and I could move the world.

image.note: A long pole over a rock, a child pressing the far end to lift a boulder; delighted

pages.text: Another is the ramp, a simple slope. It is far too hard to lift a heavy drum straight up into a lorry. But push it up a sloping plank, and it rolls up almost easily. You travel a longer way, but you push far more gently. Every ramp, every hill road that winds instead of climbing straight, uses this same idea.

image.note: A heavy drum being rolled up a plank into a lorry rather than lifted; two workers, one easy push

pages.text: The wheel may be the greatest simple machine of all. Dragging a load along the ground is exhausting, because of friction. Put it on wheels and it rolls, with the friction almost gone. Almost everything that carries or moves, from a barrow to a bus, rides on this ancient, brilliant idea.

image.note: A load dragged with effort, then the same load on a wheeled barrow moving easily; contrast

pages.text: A pulley is a wheel with a rope over it, and it lets you lift a load by pulling down, which is far easier. A gear is a wheel with teeth that turns another wheel, passing on the force and changing its speed or strength. Inside a bicycle, a clock, or a great crane, these simple parts work together to do astonishing things.

image.note: A pulley lifting a bucket; two meshing gears turning; a bicycle chain and gears; mechanical, clear

pages.text: Look around and you will find these forces and machines hiding in plain sight. The door swings on a hinge, a kind of lever. The tap turns on a screw, which is really a ramp wrapped round and round. The car rides on wheels, brakes with friction, and stays on the road because of gravity. The whole made world runs on a handful of simple ideas.

image.note: A cutaway of an ordinary room, arrows pointing out the hidden levers, ramps, screws and wheels

pages.text: So the next time you lift a lid, ride in a bus, or push open a heavy gate, you will know the secret. A force is a push or a pull. Gravity holds you down and friction slows you, and clever machines let a small effort move a mighty load. With these few ideas, humans learned to build a whole world.

image.note: A child pushing open a big estate gate with ease, arrows showing the lever at work; confident, closing
